intro.html: Some people check every detail twice; others barely look. This topic gives you words for both. Six of them describe great care (one of them, fastidious, often pokes fun at too much of it), and four describe care that is missing.

Careful: meticulous, scrupulous, diligent, assiduous, fastidious, punctilious. Careless: negligent, remiss, cursory, perfunctory. The careless words differ in how they fall short: negligent and remiss fail a duty, cursory is hasty, and perfunctory is done without interest.

words.def: very careful about every small detail
words.ex: Lila keeps a {meticulous} record of every bird she sees, with the date, the time and the weather.
words.ctx: Felix’s first sketches were messy, but his final map was {meticulous}: every street was labeled, every tree was drawn and not one line was out of place.
words.etym: From Latin meticulosus, “timid, fearful,” from metus (fear). A meticulous worker is careful, as if afraid of the smallest mistake.

mn.cue: me-TICK-ulous: every box gets a TICK
mn.text: Maya puts a tick next to every item on her packing list, then checks each one twice: she is {meticulous}.

scene.alt: A teenage girl checks off every item on her packing list beside a neat suitcase.

words.def: very careful to do what is right, or to get every detail exact
words.ex: The {scrupulous} cashier ran after a customer to give back a dime of extra change.
words.ctx: The judge at the baking contest was {scrupulous}: she would not taste her own niece’s pie, so that no one could ever say she had been unfair.
words.etym: From Latin scrupulosus, from scrupulus, “a small sharp stone”: a worry that pricks the mind like a pebble in a shoe.

mn.text: Jamal checks every single screw on Kai’s bike, twice, before he says it is safe to ride: he is {scrupulous}.

scene.alt: A man kneels with a wrench, checking every screw on a bike while a boy in a helmet waits.

words.def: working hard and steadily, with care
words.ex: A {diligent} student, Sami reviews his notes every night, not just the night before a test.
words.ctx: The garden thrived because Granny Mae was {diligent}: she weeded every morning, watered every evening and never skipped a day, even in the heat.
words.etym: From Latin diligens, from diligere, “to value, to love”: a diligent worker cares about the work.

mn.text: Omar digs and plants all day, row after row, rain or shine. The hardworking gent is {diligent}.

scene.alt: A gardener in a straw hat digs hard in the sun beside a neat row of flowers he has planted.

words.def: giving steady, careful attention to a task without letting up
words.ex: Thanks to {assiduous} practice, Rosa finally played the whole piece without a single mistake.
words.ctx: The puppy learned to sit in a week, but only because of Dev’s {assiduous} training: ten short lessons a day, with a treat for every success.
words.etym: From Latin assiduus, from assidere, “to sit beside”: ad (near) + sedere (to sit). An assiduous worker stays seated at the task.

mn.text: Lin sits beside her thousand-piece puzzle hour after hour, fitting piece after piece, and never leaves her seat. Her work is {assiduous}.

scene.alt: A woman sits at a table working steadily on a big puzzle while the clock shows the hours passing.

words.def: very fussy about details, neatness or cleanliness; hard to please
words.ex: The {fastidious} cat refused to eat from a bowl with a single crumb in it.
words.ctx: Most of the campers didn’t mind a little mud, but Victor was {fastidious}: he wiped his boots after every few steps and folded his sleeping bag into a perfect square.
words.etym: From Latin fastidiosus, “squeamish, hard to please,” from fastidium, “disgust.”

mn.text: Victor tidies fast and often: one crumb on the café table, and out comes the broom. He is {fastidious}.

scene.alt: A fussy man rushes to sweep up a single crumb in a café while a woman laughs.

words.def: very careful to follow the exact rules of proper behavior
words.ex: The {punctilious} host greeted every guest by name and seated each one by the place card.
words.ctx: Grandpa Gus is {punctilious} about manners: he stands when a guest comes in, writes a note for every gift and never starts eating before the cook sits down.
words.etym: From punctilio, a fine point of manners, from Italian puntiglio and Spanish puntillo, “a small point,” from Latin punctum, “point.”

mn.text: Professor Edwin bows just so, pours the tea just so and sets each spoon just so: every small point of manners is right. He is {punctilious}.

scene.alt: An old professor in a bow tie bows politely to a grandmother over a neat tea table.

words.def: failing to take the care you should
words.ex: The {negligent} landlord ignored the broken stair for months.
words.ctx: The night guard was found {negligent}: he had dozed through his whole shift while the alarm light on the back door blinked for three hours.
words.etym: From Latin neglegens, from neglegere, “to disregard, to fail to care for,” the same source as neglect.

mn.text: The gent dozes on the park bench while his dog digs up the flower bed: he neglects the dog he should be watching. He is {negligent}.

scene.alt: A man dozes on a park bench while his dog digs up the flowers next to a No Digging sign.

words.def: careless about a duty; failing to do what you should
words.ex: I would be {remiss} if I didn’t thank the volunteers who set up all the chairs.
words.ctx: The coach admitted that he had been {remiss}: he had forgotten to check the team’s helmets before the game, and two of them turned out to be cracked.
words.etym: From Latin remissus, “slack, relaxed,” from remittere, “to send back, to let go, to ease off.”

mn.text: Taking out the trash is Dev’s job, but he missed it Monday and missed it again Tuesday. He has been {remiss}.

scene.alt: A teen shrugs beside an overflowing, smelly trash can while his mother scolds him for missing his chore.

words.def: quick and not thorough; done in a hurry
words.ex: A {cursory} glance at the menu told Kai there was no pizza.
words.ctx: The inspector’s check was only {cursory}; she spent two minutes in a building that needed two hours, and she missed the cracked pipe in the basement.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin cursorius, “of running, swift,” from Latin cursor, “a runner.”
words.note: Cursory has nothing to do with cursing. It comes from the Latin for running, like cursor and current.

mn.text: Pip runs past every painting in the museum, giving each one half a second: his look is {cursory}.

scene.alt: A boy races past the paintings in a museum while the guide calls for him to look.

words.def: done only as a routine, with little care or interest
words.ex: Jonah gave his aunt a {perfunctory} wave without looking up from his book.
words.ctx: Her thank-you note was {perfunctory}: just “Thanks for the gift,” with no word about what the gift was or whether she liked it.
words.etym: From Late Latin perfunctorius, from perfungi, “to get through with”: per (through) + fungi (to perform).

mn.cue: per-FUNK-tory: no FUN, just get THROUGH it
mn.text: Rosa plays “Happy Birthday” with a blank face, no fun and no feeling, only to get through it. Her playing is {perfunctory}.

scene.alt: A bored teen plays the piano with a blank face while a girl in a party hat looks let down.

after.cap: Six kinds of care, and four ways to fall short.

after.html: Scrupulous has two sides. A scrupulous editor checks every comma (care with details); a scrupulous shopkeeper never cheats a customer (care about right and wrong). Its opposite, unscrupulous, almost always means dishonest. And cursory has nothing to do with cursing: it comes from Latin cursor, a runner, so a cursory look runs right past things.

opts.s: After a {cursory} glance at the instructions, Kai began building the shelf and soon had three pieces left over.
opts.why: A quick, careless glance explains the leftover pieces: it was cursory.

items.q: In which sentence does scrupulous mean careful about right and wrong?
choices: The scrupulous shopkeeper gave back the extra ten dollars a customer paid by mistake.
The scrupulous editor checked every comma in the book.
The scrupulous builder measured each board three times.
The scrupulous painter cleaned each brush after every color.
items.why: Returning money that isn’t yours is about honesty. The other sentences use scrupulous in its other sense: careful with details.

items.q: True or false: cursory comes from the same Latin word as curse.
items.why: False. Cursory comes from Latin cursor, a runner (as in current and cursor): a cursory look runs right past things.

items.q: At the end of the play, the director said, “I would be ______ if I did not thank our stage crew.” Which word fits?
items.why: Forgetting to thank the crew would be failing a duty, so she would be remiss.

items.q: Which word most often hints that someone is too fussy?
items.why: Fastidious often suggests being hard to please about neatness, cleanliness or small details. Diligent, assiduous and scrupulous praise steady, honest care.

items.q: Type the word, from Latin for “sit beside,” that means giving steady, careful attention to a task.
items.why: Assiduous comes from Latin assidere, to sit beside: an assiduous worker stays at the task.
